paras: The threatened lynching of Clifton Holden took place at Redwood Falls, Minnesota, on November 26, 1888, when townspeople angered by the murder of his cousin, the Morton barber Frank Dodge, were expected to take him from the village lockup. Warned of trouble, Sheriff Mead of Redwood County moved Holden by train to the jail at New Ulm, and no harm to him was reported. Papers in St. Paul, New Ulm and as far away as Sacramento carried the story, which differed on whether a mob actually reached the prisoner.

Early on Saturday, November 24, young people returning from a dance found Dodge dead by the roadside in one of the principal streets of Redwood Falls, with a bullet wound in the head. He had driven in from Morton the evening before with a cousin, and wagon tracks suggested that he had been shot elsewhere and dumped from a wagon. On November 25 the cousin, Clifton Holden, was arrested on suspicion and placed in the lockup; the Globe reported blood on his clothes and on the buggy the two men had used.

According to the Globe's correspondent, an earlier acquittal, a light sentence in another murder case and a likely hung jury in the Rose case had already left citizens at "a high pitch of indignation."

On the morning of November 26 Holden signed an affidavit stating that Dodge had shot himself on the drive from Morton and that he had brought the body into town, a story the Globe said no one believed. The same day a wire dispatch from Redwood Falls reported that "Lynching is threatened and there is great excitement." Morton people were "terribly wrought up," the Globe wrote, and Sheriff Mead was warned that forenoon to expect trouble that night.

At 4:10 that afternoon the sheriff took Holden to the jail at New Ulm, along with W. H. Rose, whose jury had just been discharged after failing to agree. The correspondent called the Redwood Falls lockup "a frail wooden structure" and wrote that Holden "would have been lynched to-night had he remained here." The New Ulm Weekly Review gave a sharper version, saying Holden "barely escaped being lynched last Monday evening" and was "liberated from the mob" through the sheriff's efforts before being put on a train for Sleepy Eye.

The coroner's jury returned a verdict charging Holden with Dodge's murder, and he was held in the Brown County jail with Rose. In Rochester, where Holden had lived and his father still resided, acquaintances expressed sympathy and thought it "entirely improbable" that he had killed his cousin. A Mankato cousin of both men, E. J. Whipple, told the Free Press he believed the shooting was accidental and that Holden's nervous behavior had brought suspicion on him. No report of arrests among the would-be lynchers, or of a trial of Holden, appears in the coverage.

The St. Paul Daily Globe followed the case through Redwood Falls specials, moving from a murder mystery ("Slain by an Unknown") to the arrest and then to "Anticipated a Lynching." Its account explained the mob mood as frustration with lenient courts and reported the "universal" belief in Holden's guilt, without criticizing the threat. The New Ulm Weekly Review, whose town received the prisoner, told the story inside a district court column and credited the sheriff's "energetic efforts."

Wire versions reached the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, first as a two-line item headed "Excitement About a Murder" and then as "Five Murders," an "epidemic of murder" story that added a claim that Dodge's body had been "mutilated in a horrible manner." A news-summary paragraph printed in the Mower County Transcript, the Iowa Plain Dealer and the Kanabec County Times noted only the death and the arrest, without the lynching threat. None of the papers stated the race of Holden, Dodge or the crowd.

The Globe's same-day dispatch from Redwood Falls placed the removal in the afternoon, before any mob had gathered, while the New Ulm Weekly Review, writing two days later, described Holden as freed from a mob on Monday evening.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Clifton Holden
bases: A mob threatened to lynch a jailed murder suspect and the sheriff removed him to another county's jail to prevent it (A4, A5, A6, A9).

Holden was not killed: the sheriff took him to the New Ulm jail before the expected mob acted (A4, A9), or, in one account, freed him from a mob (A6). The threat came from a mob angered by a murder he was accused of (A4, A5).

The Globe's Redwood Falls special (A4), a separate wire dispatch (A5, A9) and the New Ulm Weekly Review (A6) all report a threatened lynching and Holden's removal to New Ulm, though they differ on whether a mob actually reached him.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Lynching was threatened amid great excitement; the sheriff, 'seeing the coming storm', hurried Holden aboard a train to New Ulm.

accounts.label: New Ulm Weekly Review

framing.detail: The St. Paul Globe headlined 'Anticipated a Lynching' and explained the anger by recent lenient verdicts, while also reporting 'the opinion is universal that he shot Dodge'.
The Sacramento Record-Union ran the threat as 'Excitement About a Murder' and later as 'Five Murders', an 'epidemic of murder' story.
The New Ulm Weekly Review reported the escape in a court column and credited 'the energetic efforts' of the sheriff.

versions.value: Holden was removed in the afternoon before any mob formed; the lynching was anticipated, not attempted.
The sheriff 'liberated' Holden 'from the mob' on Monday evening.

conflicts.note: The Globe's same-day Redwood Falls dispatch is the more detailed and contemporaneous source, and the wire agrees with it; the New Ulm paper wrote at second hand two days later.

info: Frank Dodge was killed on Friday night, Nov. 23, 1888, and found the next morning; the lynching threat and Holden's removal came on Monday, Nov. 26, 1888.
Redwood Falls, Minnesota; Holden was taken to the jail at New Ulm, Brown County.
Clifton Holden, cousin of the murdered man, threatened; W. H. Rose, a murder defendant held with him, was also removed.
Holden was arrested on suspicion of shooting his cousin Frank Dodge; the coroner's jury charged him with the murder.
Unnamed townspeople; Morton people were 'terribly wrought up' and citizens of the town and county were aroused; one paper speaks of 'the mob'.
Holden was held in the Brown County jail; no report of a trial or verdict was found.
